title: 750 Teens Jump Into Dirt Pits — And It's a National Championship!
summary:
Have you ever squished wet dirt in your hands just to see how fast water runs through it? For about 750 teenagers, that's a sport! Every year, high school students from all over the country travel to windy fields in Oklahoma for the National Land and Range Judging Contest. Their mission: look at dirt—really closely—and decide if it's good for growing crops, grazing animals, or building houses.

This isn't just playing in the mud. Students climb into deep pits to examine layers of soil. They check the color, feel the texture, and even squirt water on handfuls of dirt to test permeability (how fast water soaks in). They have 25 minutes at each of four secret locations to make their best guesses. Experts have already judged the same spots, and the students who come closest to the pros' answers win.

Clay Cash, a freshman from eastern Kentucky, has been judging soil since fourth grade. He lives on a farm, so knowing how fertile the ground is matters a lot to his family. Last year, his team won the Kentucky state championship, which qualified them for this national contest. They drove 15 hours to get there! "It's a very big deal for me," Clay said. His sister had tried to make it before, and he was proud to fulfill that dream.

Maddie Willis, a junior from Indiana, loves the contest too. "I love being able to say that I play in dirt," she said. She also enjoys meeting kids from around the world and making new friends.

Soil expert DeAnn Presley says understanding dirt is key for farming, building, and even deciding where to put a railroad track. The contest has been around for almost 75 years. Coordinator Larry Wright says the skills students learn are valuable for careers in farming, environmental science, and engineering. So next time you see a patch of dirt, remember: there's a whole world under your feet, and some kids are champions at reading it.
why_it_matters: Next time you see dirt or mud, remember that it's not just messy stuff—it helps grow your food and the places you live, and understanding it can lead to exciting jobs one day.

background_read: Soil is one of Earth's most important resources, used to grow food, filter water, and support buildings.
In the 1930s, poor farming methods led to the Dust Bowl, when terrible dust storms destroyed farmland in states like Oklahoma, where the contest is held.
Today, scientists and farmers use soil science to prevent erosion and grow more food to feed the world.
